Global transition graphs are established in sequential recommendation: [GCL4SR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14837) aggregates users’ interaction sequences into a weighted item-transition graph. However, a graph containing the current training target can provide an answer-dependent shortcut. [SpotTarget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00899) demonstrates that training target-link inclusion causes overfitting and train–inference distribution shift, especially for low-degree nodes; including held-out target links causes evaluation leakage. Training-target self-counting therefore warrants scrutiny even when validation interactions are excluded correctly.

Suggested diagnostic, inferred from these findings: compare the original graph against target-occurrence subtraction and user-level cross-fitting, constructing each training user’s graph features from other users’ training histories. Subtract contributions before normalization or pruning; remove an edge only when its remaining count becomes zero. Report margins separately for singleton transitions and transitions supported by multiple users. These are proposed ablations, not a verified cross-fitting recipe from the cited papers; improved training margins alone cannot establish generalization.

Popularity is a separate shortcut. [Implicit degree bias in link prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14985) shows that standard edge sampling can strongly favor degree-based predictors, sometimes making a degree-only baseline nearly optimal. For this benchmark, useful controls are popularity-only ranking, transition-only ranking, removing the graph branch, and validation results stratified by target popularity and transition support. Keep the pinned candidate sets and macro HR@10 unchanged; treat stratified diagnostics as explanations, not replacement selection metrics.
